full_judgment:
This rule at the instance of the petitioner was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause why the judgment and order dated 3.12.75 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Comilla in Misc. Appeal No. 133 of 1975 dismissing the appeal and confirming the judgment and order dated 30.5.75 passed by the learned Munsif, 3rd Court, Comilla and Rent Controller in Misc. Case No. 5 of 1974 under Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 should not be set aside. 

 2. The case of the petitioner is that he filed an application on 14.1.74 before the Rent Controller seeking permission to deposit lent with the Rent Controller in respect of the suit premises. The application was registered as Misc. Case No. 5 of 1974. The prayer was opposed by the landlord opposite party. 

 The Rent Controller considered the prayer and holding the petitioner as habitual defaulter rejected the prayer for depositing the rent. 

 3. Being Aggrieved by the aforesaid order the petitioner filed Misc. Appeal No. 133 of 1975. The appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, who dismissed the appeal and confirmed the order of the Rent Controller. 

 4. Mr. S.C. Das, the learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner is that the landlord used to realize rent for 2 or 3 months at a time and that the landlord did not take rent for month. When the tenant offered rent for Ashar, 1379 B.S., the landlord told him that he would take rent of several months at a time and pay up his municipal dues. Thus, at the instance of the landlord there had been accumulation of 18 months' rent upto Agrahayan 1380 BS. The petitioner subsequently offered the rent to the landlord but on his refusal the petitioner smelt something wrong. So he sent the rent by money order but the landlord did not accept it. He, furthermore, applied to the Rent Controller to deposit the rent but the Rent Controller without giving permission to deposit the rent held that he was a defaulter and he had no right to deposit rent. The learned Advocate submits that it was for the Rent Controller to consider whether the tenant tendered rent to the landlord, whether the landlord refused to accept the rent, whether after the refusal the tenant sent the rent by postal money order and whether the landlord refused to accept the money order and whether within a fortnight after the refusal by the landlord to accept the rent sent by money order, the tenant applied for permission to deposit the rent. It has further been submitted that it is not within the jurisdiction of the Rent Controller to decide whether the tenant is a defaulter or not. If the Rent Controller decides that the tenant is a defaulter then it will prejudice the tenant in a future suit if filed by the landlord for ejectment of the tenant on the ground of being a defaulter. The learned Advocate, therefore, submits that the findings and decision of the lower Appellate Court is illegal and liable to be set aside. In this connection the learned Advocate has referred to the decision in the case of Md. Aktar Vs. Md. Abdus Siddique (1956) & DLR 272 wherein it has been held that the question of default is not to be determined by the Rent Collector at the time of deciding the prayer for permission to deposit rent. It has been submitted that the Rent Controller is bound to accept the rent tendered by the tenant for deposit. 

 5. Mr. Shahabuddin, the learned Advocate, appearing for the opposite party submits that there was no arrangement between the opposite party submits that there was no arrangement between the opposite party landlord and petitioner tenant that the landlord would accept rent for 2/3 months at a time. That the landlord did not ask the tenant that he would receive rent for several months and clear up his municipal dues. The learned Advocate however, submits that the tenant sent 18 months' rent at a time to the landlord by money order. The landlord undoubtedly refused to accept the rent sent by money order as he was already a defaulter. It has been submitted that the tenant was habitual defaulter and as such the opposite party landlord has filed S.C.C. suit 611 of 1976 for ejectment of the tenant. The suit of course has been stayed. In the above circumstances the learned Advocate submits that the learned District Judge rightly dismissed the appeal. It has been submitted that there is no ground for an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure as the learned District Judge did not act illegally or with material irregularity in dismissing the appeal. The learned District Judge did not believe petitioner's allegation that the landlord used to take rent for 2/3 months at a time, that the landlord asked the tenant that he would take rent after several months so that be might pay up the Municipal Tax. 

 6. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the rent receipts show that rent was accepted by the landlord for several months each time. On the other hand, the submission of the leaned Advocate for the opposite party is that he being a habitual defaulter paid rent for several months at a time and the landlord accepted it. 

 7. Both the courts below concurrently found that the tenant paid rent 2/3 months at a time. The Rent Controller in view of the prayer for permission to deposit rent for 18 months at a time held that the petitioner is not entitled to deposit rent as he has been already a defaulter. The learned District Judge also confirmed the decision of the Rent Controller. In the case referred to above in 8 D.L.R. page 272 it has been decided that the Rent Controller is to accept rent offered by the tenant for deposit without determining the question whether the tenant is defaulter or not. It has, however, not been decided in, that case whether the tenant is entitled to deposit rent for several months at a time although in that case rent for several months was tendered. In the case before us 18 months rent was accumulated. The same was sent by money order but the landlord did not accept it. Thereafter the tenant applied to the Rent Controller for permission to deep sit the rent. Under Section 19(A) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance the provision is that the tenant may deposit such rent within a fortnight of the date on which the rent so remitted is returned by the postal authority as undelivered. It appears that the rent referred to is monthly rent i.e. each month rent offered to the landlord within the specific period and refused by the landlord to accept it and the rent sent by money order is returned to the tenant as undelivered. The tenant is required to deposit the rent within a fortnight from the day on which the money order refused by the landlord was returned to him by the postal authority as refused or as undelivered. If the tenant does not deposit the rent within a for night from the date of return of the money order to him undelivered the tenant is not entitled to deposit thereafter. Otherwise the words within a fortnight becomes meaningless. The learned Advocate for opposite party has referred to the decision in the case of Ramjan Ali Mistry Vs. Md. Hedayetullah (1979) 31 D.L.R. (AD) 183 wherein it has been held that when the conditions under section 18 and 19 are fulfilled the tenant is entitled to protection and that the law makes no distinction between default for one month or doe fault for more than one month or a habitual defaulter. When the conditions of section 19 are not fulfilled the tenant is not entitled to deposit rent in time and such a deposit is not a valid deposit. In view of the above position the law does not empower the Rent Controller to come to a finding in an application for deposit of rent to hold that the tenant is a defaulter but the Rent Controller in view of section 19(a) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance can come to a finding that the tenant has not come within the specific period to deposit the rent In such circumstances there does not appear any bar on his refusal to accept the rent. In 8 D.L.R. case referred to above there is no discussion and finding to the effect that the tenant can apply for deposit of several months' rent which was previously sent to the landlord at a time and the landlord refused to accent the rent and the postal authority sent back the money order to the tenant as undelivered or refused. 

 8. The findings of the courts below that the tenant petitioner did not come to deposit the rent in time is a finding of fact and it cannot be disturbed in a case under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It does not appear that the learned District Judge acted illegally and with material irregularity in exercise of his jurisdiction in dismissing the appeal. The findings of the learned District Judge that the petitioner tenant is a defaulter will not prejudice the petitioner tenant in the suit for eviction. With this observation, I am of the opinion that there is nothing to interfere in this case.
